Planning a safe roadworks site visit

Published

Before you go

This is invented guidance text used only to give a test page a long body. It does not describe any real requirement, and nobody should rely on it. A site visit is easier to plan when you know why you are going, who will be there and what you need to see. Write down the purpose in a sentence or two so that everyone who attends shares the same aim.

Find out who controls the site and ask for their arrival instructions in good time. Most sites have a gate, a signing-in point and a briefing, and each of these can take longer than people expect. Allow enough time at the start of the visit so that you are not rushed through the briefing, because a rushed briefing is when details get missed.

Check what personal protective equipment is required and make sure you have it with you, in good condition, and that it fits. Items that are shared or borrowed at the gate are often the wrong size. Bring spare gloves and a high-visibility jacket that meets the standard the site asks for, and check the weather forecast for the day so that you can dress for it.

Tell someone who is not attending where you are going and when you expect to be back. Agree a simple way of checking in, such as a message when you arrive and another when you leave. If you are visiting alone, agree what the other person will do if they do not hear from you at the time you said.

Read any documents the site sends ahead of the visit. These usually include a plan of the area, a list of hazards and the arrangements for traffic management. Mark anything you do not understand and ask about it before the day, because the site team will have more time to answer before the visit than during it.

Decide what you want to record and how you will record it. Photographs are useful, but sites often have rules about where you may take them and who may appear in them. Ask before you take any, and keep notes on paper as well so that you are not relying on a single device that may run out of charge in the cold.

On site

Arrive a little early and sign in as asked. Listen carefully to the briefing and ask about anything that differs from what you were told beforehand. Locate the welfare facilities, the first aid point and the emergency assembly area before you walk anywhere, and make a mental note of the route back to the gate.

Stay with your escort and keep to the marked walkways. Do not step into a live traffic lane, even briefly, to get a better view. If you need to see something that is outside the safe route, say so and let the site team decide whether it can be arranged safely, perhaps at a different time or from a different place.

Pay attention to moving plant and vehicles. Make eye contact with drivers and operators before you cross their path, and wait until they have acknowledged you. Be aware of reversing vehicles, which can be hard to hear in a noisy work area, and of the blind spots that large machines have around them.

Take your notes as you go and record the time. A short note made at the moment is worth more than a long note written from memory in the evening. Write down the names of the people you speak to and what they agreed to send you, so that you can follow it up without having to ask the same questions again.

If something looks unsafe, stop and say so. You do not need to be sure that it is a problem to raise it, and a good site team would rather hear a concern that turns out to be nothing than miss one that matters. Follow the instructions you are given and leave the area if you are asked to.

Keep an eye on your own condition during the visit. Long days outdoors are tiring, and tiredness makes mistakes more likely. Drink water, take any breaks that are offered, and tell your escort if you need to stop. It is better to cut a visit short than to carry on when you are not at your best.

After the visit

Sign out as asked and hand back any equipment you borrowed. Before you leave the area, check that you have everything you brought with you and that your notes and photographs are safe. If you saw anything that needs reporting, do it before you go, while the details are fresh and the right people are still on site.

Write up your notes within a day or two. Include what you saw, what you learned and what you will do differently as a result. Keep the write-up short and factual, and separate what you observed from what you were told, because the two can be easy to mix up when you read them back later.

Share what is useful with your team. A short summary at a team meeting helps others learn from the visit and shows the site team that the time they gave you was put to good use. Thank the people who looked after you, and let them know if anything you learned changed how you will approach your work.

Think about what you would change about the way you planned the visit. Perhaps you needed more time, a different piece of equipment or a question you did not think to ask. Note this down while it is fresh, and use it next time. Planning a visit gets quicker with practice, and each visit is a chance to improve the next one.

Finally, record the visit in your development log if you keep one. Note the date, where you went and the main things you took away. Be honest about how long you spent learning, which may be less than the time you spent travelling and waiting. This sample text ends here.
